chapters.title: EMS Systems
chapters.hook: EMS care works as a coordinated system, not as isolated ambulance treatment.
chapters.concept: Connect medical direction, scope, quality improvement, evidence, transport decisions, and professional responsibility into one system of care.
cues: Medical direction and protocols define how care is authorized.
CQI turns field data and near misses into safer systems.
Destination choice is part of treatment, especially when specialty resources matter.
priorities: Know your role, scope, and escalation path before a call becomes complex.
Use evidence and system resources to improve both individual care and the EMS system.
pitfalls: Treating protocols as substitutes for judgment.
Confusing certification, licensure, credentialing, and local authorization.
prompts: What system resource could change this patient’s outcome?
How would you recognize a systems problem rather than an individual mistake?

chapters.title: Workforce Safety and Wellness
chapters.hook: A paramedic who is injured, exhausted, contaminated, or cognitively overloaded cannot provide reliable care.
chapters.concept: Build a safety system around PPE, lifting, exposure prevention, sleep, stress recovery, and early recognition of scene threats.
cues: Standard precautions begin before patient contact.
Fatigue and stress impair attention, communication, and decision making.
Safe lifting and movement require planning, equipment, and adequate personnel.
priorities: Pause long enough to identify hazards before entering.
Use PPE and movement strategies that match the actual risk.
pitfalls: Rushing into a scene because the patient looks critical.
Normalizing chronic sleep loss or emotional overload as part of the job.
prompts: Which hazard can hurt the crew before treatment even starts?
What changes when the provider is fatigued?

chapters.title: Public Health
chapters.hook: EMS sees patterns in communities that may not be visible inside a hospital.
chapters.concept: Think beyond the single call: surveillance, prevention, access to care, social determinants, education, and community risk reduction.
cues: Epidemiology describes patterns of illness and injury in populations.
Surveillance can identify emerging threats and clusters.
Prevention and referral can reduce future 911 use and harm.
priorities: Notice repeated patterns across patients and locations.
Connect patients to the right resource when transport alone will not solve the problem.
pitfalls: Viewing every call only as an isolated event.
Assuming prevention is outside the EMS role.
prompts: What population-level pattern might this call reveal?
What upstream factor is driving the emergency?

chapters.title: Medical, Legal, and Ethical Issues
chapters.hook: Good care must be clinically sound, legally defensible, and ethically respectful.
chapters.concept: Separate capacity from agreement, consent from compliance, and legal authority from personal preference.
cues: Decision-making capacity is task- and time-specific.
Refusal requires informed discussion, documentation, and attention to reversible causes of impaired capacity.
Confidentiality, mandatory reporting, advance directives, and evidence preservation can all affect field decisions.
priorities: Assess capacity before accepting a high-risk refusal.
Document what you found, explained, offered, and observed.
pitfalls: Equating disagreement with incapacity.
Using a signature as a substitute for a careful refusal process.
prompts: Can this patient understand, appreciate, reason, and communicate a choice?
What legal duty changes the normal confidentiality rule?

chapters.title: Communications
chapters.hook: Communication is a clinical intervention because information changes decisions.
chapters.concept: Use therapeutic communication with patients and closed-loop, structured communication with teams.
cues: Open-ended questions uncover concerns that yes/no questions miss.
Closed-loop communication reduces team errors during high-stress care.
A concise handoff prioritizes the patient’s trajectory, key findings, treatment, and response.
priorities: Match language, pace, and approach to the patient.
State critical information explicitly instead of assuming others noticed it.
pitfalls: Talking at a patient instead of with the patient.
Giving a chronological radio report that hides the most important information.
prompts: What does the receiving team need to know first?
What communication barrier could change the history you obtain?

chapters.title: Documentation
chapters.hook: The patient care report is a clinical record, communication tool, quality artifact, and legal document.
chapters.concept: Write objective, chronological documentation that explains assessment, reasoning, treatment, response, and disposition.
cues: Document observable facts and attribute statements to their source.
Include reassessment and response to interventions.
Refusals and unusual events need especially clear documentation.
priorities: Record times and trends that show how the patient changed.
Correct errors transparently according to policy.
pitfalls: Charting conclusions without supporting findings.
Using vague phrases such as “stable” without objective context.
prompts: Could another clinician reconstruct the call from the PCR?
Which omitted detail would most weaken your clinical reasoning?

chapters.title: Medical Terminology
chapters.hook: Medical language is a compression system for anatomy, physiology, disease, and procedures.
chapters.concept: Decode unfamiliar terms by roots, prefixes, suffixes, location words, and context rather than memorizing every term independently.
cues: Directional and positional terms prevent ambiguity.
Common roots often reveal the organ system or process involved.
Abbreviations can be unsafe when they are nonstandard or ambiguous.
priorities: Break unfamiliar words into meaningful parts.
Prefer plain language with patients and precise terminology with clinicians.
pitfalls: Guessing from a familiar-looking abbreviation.
Using jargon that the patient cannot understand.
prompts: What does the word root tell you before you know the full term?
When is an abbreviation more dangerous than helpful?

chapters.title: Anatomy and Physiology
chapters.hook: Assessment makes more sense when you can picture what the body is trying to do.
chapters.concept: Link structure to function: ventilation, circulation, neurologic control, metabolism, movement, and homeostasis are interdependent.
cues: Cells require oxygen delivery, substrate, waste removal, and stable internal conditions.
Organ systems compensate for one another only within limits.
Anatomic relationships help predict symptoms and injury patterns.
priorities: Translate signs into the organ function that is failing.
Use anatomy to predict hidden injury and downstream effects.
pitfalls: Memorizing structures without understanding function.
Treating each organ system as independent.
prompts: Which structure explains this sign?
What second system will fail if this problem progresses?

chapters.title: Pathophysiology
chapters.hook: Pathophysiology explains why the patient looks the way they do and what will happen next.
chapters.concept: Follow the chain from insult to cellular response to compensation to decompensation.
cues: Hypoxia, ischemia, inflammation, and metabolic failure can converge on cellular dysfunction.
Compensation can hide severe illness until reserve is exhausted.
Acid-base and perfusion changes often reflect the body’s attempt to preserve vital organs.
priorities: Ask what mechanism can produce the whole pattern, not just one abnormal vital sign.
Trend compensation signs for evidence that reserve is failing.
pitfalls: Treating numbers without understanding the process behind them.
Assuming normal blood pressure excludes shock.
prompts: What is the initiating insult?
Which compensatory mechanism is becoming exhausted?

chapters.title: Life Span Development
chapters.hook: Normal physiology, communication, risk, and presentation change across the life span.
chapters.concept: Adapt assessment and interaction to developmental stage while avoiding stereotypes.
cues: Infants and children compensate differently from adults.
Adolescents may need privacy and direct communication.
Older adults may have atypical presentations, reduced reserve, and complex medication effects.
priorities: Use age-appropriate expectations for vital signs and behavior.
Engage caregivers without speaking around the patient.
pitfalls: Treating a child as a small adult.
Attributing abnormal findings to “just aging.”
prompts: What is normal for this developmental stage?
How should your communication change for this patient?

chapters.title: Patient Assessment
chapters.hook: Assessment is a repeating decision loop, not a one-time checklist.
chapters.concept: Move from scene safety to primary threats, focused history and exam, working impression, treatment, and reassessment.
cues: The primary assessment finds immediate threats and determines urgency.
History and focused examination refine the differential.
Reassessment tests whether your working diagnosis and treatment are still valid.
priorities: Correct life threats as they are found.
Use trends in mental status, work of breathing, perfusion, and vital signs.
pitfalls: Completing a full history before correcting an immediate threat.
Failing to change the plan when the patient changes.
prompts: What can kill this patient in the next few minutes?
Which new finding should force you to revise your impression?

chapters.title: Critical Thinking and Clinical Decision Making
chapters.hook: Expert judgment is disciplined pattern recognition plus deliberate checking for alternatives.
chapters.concept: Recognize cues, analyze them, form and rank hypotheses, choose actions, and evaluate the response while guarding against bias.
cues: Anchoring makes the first explanation feel more certain than it is.
A differential diagnosis is ranked by likelihood and danger.
New data should increase or decrease confidence in competing hypotheses.
priorities: Name at least one dangerous alternative before committing.
Use treatment response as new diagnostic information.
pitfalls: Premature closure after one plausible diagnosis.
Seeking only evidence that confirms the first impression.
prompts: What finding does not fit your leading diagnosis?
What dangerous diagnosis is less likely but cannot be missed?

chapters.title: Principles of Pharmacology
chapters.hook: Medication effects depend on the drug, dose, route, receptor, patient, and physiologic state.
chapters.concept: Connect pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications, interactions, and adverse effects to the actual patient.
cues: Pharmacodynamics describes what a drug does to the body.
Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to a drug.
Organ dysfunction and interacting drugs can change expected effects.
priorities: Know the intended physiologic effect before administration.
Reassess for both therapeutic effect and harm.
pitfalls: Giving a familiar medication without checking contraindications.
Assuming a drug effect will be identical in every patient.
prompts: What physiologic target are you trying to change?
Which patient factor could amplify or blunt this drug?

chapters.title: Medication Administration
chapters.hook: Safe medication delivery is a process, not a single act.
chapters.concept: Verify patient, medication, indication, route, concentration, dose calculation, access, administration, and reassessment.
cues: Different routes change onset, reliability, and risk.
IV and IO access are tools with distinct advantages and complications.
Medication math should be checked in a repeatable way.
priorities: Read labels and concentrations before drawing up medication.
Use a second check for high-risk calculations when feasible.
pitfalls: Confusing concentration with total amount.
Skipping reassessment after a technically successful administration.
prompts: What is the concentration in the container?
Which route is reliable for this patient right now?

chapters.title: Emergency Medications
chapters.hook: Emergency medications are best learned by clinical problem and physiologic goal, not by isolated lists.
chapters.concept: Organize medications by what problem they solve, when they are dangerous, and what response should be expected.
cues: Resuscitation drugs support specific physiologic goals.
Analgesia, sedation, bronchodilation, glucose management, and antidotes all require reassessment.
Local scope and protocol determine specific drug choices and dosing.
priorities: State the indication and desired endpoint before administration.
Use your local protocol for exact dosing and repeat intervals.
pitfalls: Memorizing doses without understanding indications.
Administering a medication because it is “on the protocol” despite a contraindication.
prompts: What endpoint tells you the medication worked?
What finding would make you withhold or change the medication?

chapters.title: Airway Management
chapters.hook: Airway management is oxygenation and ventilation management—not merely placement of a tube.
chapters.concept: Progress from positioning and basic maneuvers to oxygenation, BVM technique, adjuncts, supraglottic devices, intubation, capnography, and rescue plans.
cues: A patent airway does not guarantee adequate ventilation.
Two-person BVM technique often improves seal and tidal volume.
Waveform capnography helps confirm and monitor advanced airway ventilation.
priorities: Optimize positioning, suction, oxygenation, and BVM before escalating.
Always have a failed-airway rescue plan.
pitfalls: Fixating on intubation while oxygenation deteriorates.
Accepting tube placement without continuous physiologic confirmation.
prompts: Is the problem airway patency, oxygenation, ventilation, or all three?
What is your next best rescue if the first airway plan fails?

chapters.title: Respiratory Emergencies
chapters.hook: Dyspnea is a symptom; the job is to identify the mechanism of respiratory failure.
chapters.concept: Differentiate obstructive, restrictive, infectious, vascular, cardiogenic, and ventilatory causes using work of breathing, breath sounds, history, gas exchange, and trajectory.
cues: Asthma and COPD create obstructive airflow problems but may require different context.
Pulmonary edema often reflects cardiac failure and fluid shift.
A “quiet chest,” fatigue, altered mentation, or falling ventilation can signal impending arrest.
priorities: Support oxygenation and ventilation while refining the cause.
Escalate ventilatory support before exhaustion becomes arrest.
pitfalls: Assuming wheezing always means asthma.
Using pulse oximetry alone to judge ventilation.
prompts: Is this primarily oxygenation failure or ventilatory failure?
Which sign suggests the patient is tiring?

chapters.title: Cardiovascular Emergencies
chapters.hook: Cardiac care combines perfusion assessment, electrical interpretation, ischemia recognition, and time-sensitive intervention.
chapters.concept: Read the patient and the monitor together: stability, rate, rhythm, conduction, ischemia, pump failure, and perfusion all matter.
cues: A rhythm is clinically important when it changes perfusion.
Serial 12-lead ECGs can reveal evolving ischemia.
Unstable brady- and tachydysrhythmias require faster intervention than stable ones.
priorities: Identify instability before naming every rhythm detail.
Correlate ECG findings with symptoms, pulses, blood pressure, and perfusion.
pitfalls: Treating the monitor rather than the patient.
Missing right ventricular or posterior involvement when the clinical pattern suggests it.
prompts: Is the patient stable or unstable because of this rhythm?
What does the 12-lead add to the bedside assessment?

chapters.title: Neurologic Emergencies
chapters.hook: Neurologic emergencies require fast pattern recognition without forgetting metabolic and toxic mimics.
chapters.concept: Use level of consciousness, focal deficits, seizure history, pupils, glucose, time course, and airway protection to organize the problem.
cues: Stroke systems depend on last-known-well and rapid recognition.
Seizure, hypoglycemia, intoxication, and postictal states can mimic stroke.
Declining mental status can threaten ventilation before oxygen saturation falls.
priorities: Establish timing and screen for reversible mimics early.
Protect oxygenation and ventilation while expediting appropriate destination.
pitfalls: Labeling every altered patient as intoxicated.
Delaying transport to complete an overly detailed neurologic exam.
prompts: What is the last known well?
Which reversible mimic can be checked immediately?

chapters.title: Diseases of the Eyes, Ears, Nose, and Throat
chapters.hook: Small anatomic spaces can produce disproportionate pain, bleeding, airway risk, and functional loss.
chapters.concept: Recognize vision-threatening, airway-threatening, severe bleeding, infectious, and foreign-body presentations while protecting delicate structures.
cues: Sudden visual loss is time-sensitive even when the patient otherwise looks well.
Posterior epistaxis can be significant and difficult to visualize.
Airway swelling or deep neck infection can deteriorate rapidly.
priorities: Protect the eye from pressure when globe injury is suspected.
Prioritize airway and bleeding control when ENT pathology becomes systemic.
pitfalls: Trying to remove an embedded ocular object.
Underestimating blood loss from persistent epistaxis.
prompts: Is vision, airway, or hemorrhage the immediate threat?
What maneuver could worsen an injured globe?

chapters.title: Abdominal and Gastrointestinal Emergencies
chapters.hook: Abdominal complaints are often diagnostic uncertainty problems with hidden bleeding or inflammation.
chapters.concept: Use location, onset, character, associated symptoms, exam, perfusion, and risk factors to identify dangerous patterns without overclaiming a diagnosis.
cues: GI bleeding can be occult yet hemodynamically important.
Peritoneal irritation suggests significant intra-abdominal pathology.
Older adults and immunocompromised patients may have muted findings.
priorities: Treat shock and symptoms while transporting for definitive evaluation.
Trend perfusion and mental status, not pain score alone.
pitfalls: Ruling out serious disease because the abdomen is not dramatically tender.
Withholding appropriate analgesia solely to preserve the exam.
prompts: Could this be bleeding even without obvious blood?
What finding suggests peritoneal irritation or poor perfusion?

chapters.title: Genitourinary and Renal Emergencies
chapters.hook: Renal and genitourinary problems can quickly become electrolyte, volume, infectious, or bleeding emergencies.
chapters.concept: Connect urinary symptoms and dialysis history to fluid balance, acid-base status, potassium risk, infection, and access complications.
cues: Dialysis patients can have major potassium and fluid abnormalities.
Missed dialysis changes the differential for dyspnea, weakness, and dysrhythmia.
Flank pain, hematuria, fever, and shock point toward different levels of urgency.
priorities: Protect dialysis access and gather treatment timing.
Look for ECG and perfusion evidence of systemic complications.
pitfalls: Treating renal colic as benign when fever or shock is present.
Using a dialysis fistula for routine access without authorization.
prompts: When was the last dialysis session?
Is this local urinary disease or a systemic electrolyte/volume problem?

chapters.title: Gynecologic Emergencies
chapters.hook: Gynecologic emergencies combine bleeding, infection, pregnancy-related risk, pain, and sensitive communication.
chapters.concept: Approach vaginal bleeding and pelvic pain with privacy, trauma-informed care, pregnancy consideration, perfusion assessment, and broad differential diagnosis.
cues: Ectopic pregnancy can cause life-threatening internal bleeding.
Pelvic infection can become systemic.
Sexual assault care requires consent, privacy, evidence awareness, and emotional support.
priorities: Assess pregnancy possibility and hemorrhage risk early.
Preserve patient autonomy during sensitive examination and history.
pitfalls: Assuming all vaginal bleeding is menstrual.
Collecting unnecessary details during a sexual assault evaluation.
prompts: Could pregnancy change the risk of this presentation?
What can you do to preserve control and dignity for the patient?

chapters.title: Endocrine Emergencies
chapters.hook: Endocrine emergencies often present as altered mental status, dehydration, shock, temperature change, or dysrhythmia.
chapters.concept: Use glucose, history, hydration, breathing pattern, medication use, and endocrine clues to distinguish rapid glucose problems from slower metabolic crises.
cues: Hypoglycemia can cause abrupt neurologic dysfunction.
DKA and hyperosmolar states produce dehydration and metabolic stress over time.
Thyroid and adrenal crises can produce shock and extreme physiologic changes.
priorities: Check glucose early in altered patients.
Treat airway, breathing, circulation, and perfusion while addressing the endocrine cause.
pitfalls: Stopping the assessment after finding an abnormal glucose.
Assuming every hyperglycemic patient is in DKA.
prompts: Does the time course fit hypoglycemia or a hyperglycemic crisis?
What other illness may have triggered the endocrine decompensation?

chapters.title: Hematologic Emergencies
chapters.hook: Blood disorders alter oxygen carrying, clotting, viscosity, immune function, or microvascular flow.
chapters.concept: Recognize bleeding tendency, anemia, sickle-cell complications, transfusion reactions, and malignancy-related vulnerability as systemic problems.
cues: Sickle-cell crises can involve severe pain, acute chest syndrome, stroke, or infection.
Coagulopathy changes the significance of even minor trauma.
Anemia can reduce oxygen delivery despite a normal saturation reading.
priorities: Ask about anticoagulants, bleeding disorders, transfusions, and sickle-cell complications.
Treat perfusion and oxygen delivery while identifying high-risk manifestations.
pitfalls: Equating normal SpO₂ with normal oxygen content.
Underestimating minor trauma in an anticoagulated patient.
prompts: Is oxygen delivery impaired even though saturation is normal?
Which hematologic history changes the risk of this complaint?

chapters.title: Immunologic Emergencies
chapters.hook: Immune emergencies range from local allergic symptoms to rapidly fatal airway and circulatory collapse.
chapters.concept: Recognize anaphylaxis as a systemic syndrome and distinguish it from isolated skin findings while anticipating biphasic or progressive reactions.
cues: Anaphylaxis can involve airway, breathing, circulation, or multiple organ systems.
Skin findings may be absent in severe reactions.
Rapid progression after exposure should increase urgency.
priorities: Treat life-threatening airway or perfusion compromise immediately according to protocol.
Remove the trigger when possible and reassess for progression.
pitfalls: Waiting for hives before considering anaphylaxis.
Underestimating a patient who briefly improves after initial treatment.
prompts: Which organ systems are involved?
Is the reaction progressing toward airway or circulatory failure?

chapters.title: Infectious Diseases
chapters.hook: Infectious disease care combines patient resuscitation with protection of the crew and public.
chapters.concept: Use transmission route, exposure history, local prevalence, sepsis physiology, and infection-control practices to manage both individual and population risk.
cues: Droplet, airborne, contact, and bloodborne hazards require different precautions.
Sepsis is organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection, not just fever.
Older or immunocompromised patients may be severely infected without fever.
priorities: Select PPE from the suspected route of transmission.
Look for perfusion and organ dysfunction when infection is possible.
pitfalls: Using fever as the only screen for serious infection.
Removing PPE too early during decontamination or cleanup.
prompts: What transmission route is most plausible?
Is this infection causing organ dysfunction or shock?

chapters.title: Toxicology
chapters.hook: Toxicology is pattern recognition plus meticulous supportive care.
chapters.concept: Identify exposure route, toxidrome, time course, co-ingestants, decontamination needs, and immediately reversible threats before chasing an exact substance.
cues: Toxidromes group findings such as pupil size, secretions, temperature, mental status, and vital signs.
Airway and ventilation failure are common causes of death in overdose.
Scene safety and decontamination may precede patient contact.
priorities: Support ABCs first and use antidotes when the pattern and protocol support them.
Bring medication containers or reliable exposure information when safe.
pitfalls: Focusing on the substance name while ventilation fails.
Inducing vomiting or performing decontamination without indication.
prompts: Which toxidrome best fits the whole pattern?
Is there a specific antidote, or is supportive care the priority?

chapters.title: Psychiatric Emergencies
chapters.hook: Behavior is a symptom; medical, toxic, neurologic, and psychiatric causes can look alike.
chapters.concept: Balance safety, de-escalation, capacity, suicide risk, medical screening, restraint risks, and respectful communication.
cues: New agitation or confusion can be delirium from a medical cause.
Suicide assessment should be direct and specific.
Physical and chemical restraint require monitoring and ongoing reassessment.
priorities: Use verbal de-escalation and reduce stimulation when possible.
Look for hypoxia, hypoglycemia, intoxication, trauma, infection, and other reversible causes.
pitfalls: Assuming bizarre behavior is “just psychiatric.”
Using restraint as punishment or convenience.
prompts: What medical cause could mimic this behavior?
What is the least restrictive safe option?

chapters.title: Trauma Systems and Mechanism of Injury
chapters.hook: Mechanism predicts risk, but physiology and anatomy determine current urgency.
chapters.concept: Use energy transfer, anatomic injury patterns, physiologic findings, and trauma-system destination criteria together.
cues: High-energy mechanisms raise suspicion for occult injury.
Older adults and anticoagulated patients can have serious injury after modest mechanisms.
Trauma destination decisions should be made early when criteria are met.
priorities: Identify immediate threats before reconstructing the crash.
Use mechanism to guide—not replace—the physical assessment.
pitfalls: Letting dramatic vehicle damage distract from patient physiology.
Using absence of external injury to rule out internal trauma.
prompts: What energy was transferred to the patient?
Which finding matters more than the mechanism right now?

chapters.title: Bleeding
chapters.hook: Hemorrhage kills through loss of circulating volume and oxygen delivery, often before blood pressure falls.
chapters.concept: Find and control external hemorrhage while recognizing concealed bleeding and compensatory shock.
cues: Severe extremity bleeding may require immediate tourniquet use.
Pelvis, chest, abdomen, and long bones can conceal major blood loss.
Tachycardia, skin changes, mental status, and pulse quality may precede hypotension.
priorities: Control life-threatening external bleeding during the primary assessment.
Minimize scene delay for suspected internal hemorrhage.
pitfalls: Waiting for hypotension to diagnose hemorrhagic shock.
Repeatedly loosening an effective tourniquet.
prompts: Where could blood be hiding?
What sign suggests compensation is failing?

chapters.title: Soft-Tissue Trauma
chapters.hook: Soft-tissue injury ranges from superficial wounds to devastating contamination, crush, and tissue loss.
chapters.concept: Assess depth, contamination, bleeding, neurovascular status, mechanism, and the risk to underlying structures.
cues: Open wounds can hide tendon, vessel, nerve, or organ injury.
Crush injury can cause systemic metabolic complications.
Impaled objects usually stabilize rather than remove in the field.
priorities: Control bleeding and protect tissue while preserving function.
Document distal motor, sensory, and circulatory findings when limb injury is involved.
pitfalls: Focusing on wound appearance while missing deeper injury.
Removing an impaled object without a compelling reason.
prompts: What deeper structure may be injured beneath this wound?
Is this a local wound or a systemic crush problem?

chapters.title: Burns
chapters.hook: Burn severity depends on depth, extent, location, mechanism, inhalation injury, patient factors, and associated trauma.
chapters.concept: Prioritize airway risk, remove ongoing exposure, estimate extent, prevent hypothermia, and identify chemical, electrical, or circumferential complications.
cues: Airway edema may progress after facial or inhalation injury.
Electrical burns can cause deep injury disproportionate to skin findings.
Large burns disrupt temperature control and fluid balance.
priorities: Stop the burning process while protecting rescuers.
Anticipate airway deterioration early rather than waiting for complete obstruction.
pitfalls: Cooling large burns so aggressively that the patient becomes hypothermic.
Judging electrical injury only by the size of skin burns.
prompts: Is the airway likely to worsen?
Does the mechanism imply deeper injury than the skin shows?

chapters.title: Face and Neck Trauma
chapters.hook: Face and neck injuries can threaten airway, vision, major vessels, and the cervical structures simultaneously.
chapters.concept: Control bleeding, suction aggressively when needed, protect the airway, evaluate eye injury, and anticipate swelling or expanding hematoma.
cues: Facial bleeding can rapidly obstruct the airway.
Neck trauma can injure airway, esophagus, vessels, and spinal structures.
Eye trauma requires protection from pressure and further injury.
priorities: Position and suction to maintain airway patency while protecting the spine when indicated.
Escalate airway planning early when swelling or distorted anatomy is progressing.
pitfalls: Letting blood pool in the airway while preparing advanced equipment.
Applying pressure directly to a suspected globe rupture.
prompts: What will make this airway harder in five minutes?
Is bleeding external, airway-threatening, or both?

chapters.title: Head and Spine Trauma
chapters.hook: The priorities are preventing secondary brain injury and identifying neurologic compromise without causing additional harm.
chapters.concept: Use mental status, pupils, motor findings, mechanism, ventilation, perfusion, and spinal findings to guide care and destination.
cues: Hypoxia and hypotension worsen traumatic brain injury.
Abnormal posturing, declining GCS, or unequal pupils can signal worsening intracranial pathology.
Spinal motion restriction should be based on assessment and mechanism, not automatic immobilization of everyone.
priorities: Protect oxygenation, ventilation, and perfusion.
Trend neurologic findings and expedite transport for deterioration.
pitfalls: Hyperventilating routinely without signs of impending herniation.
Focusing on the spine while missing airway or perfusion failure.
prompts: What secondary insult can you prevent right now?
Is the neurologic exam improving, stable, or worsening?

chapters.title: Chest Trauma
chapters.hook: Chest trauma can impair ventilation, oxygenation, circulation, or all three within minutes.
chapters.concept: Differentiate open pneumothorax, tension physiology, hemothorax, tamponade, pulmonary contusion, and chest-wall injury using mechanics and perfusion.
cues: Tension physiology is a clinical diagnosis of obstructive shock, not a radiographic one.
Pulmonary contusion may worsen over time.
Chest injury can cause major internal blood loss with little external evidence.
priorities: Treat immediately reversible life threats during the primary assessment.
Reassess after every chest intervention because physiology can change quickly.
pitfalls: Waiting for a classic late sign before treating a crashing patient.
Assuming normal initial lung sounds exclude evolving injury.
prompts: Is the dominant problem ventilation or obstructive/hemorrhagic shock?
What changed after your intervention?

chapters.title: Abdominal and Genitourinary Trauma
chapters.hook: Abdominal and pelvic trauma are dangerous because major injury is often hidden.
chapters.concept: Use mechanism, pain, tenderness, distention, bruising, pelvic stability clues, GU findings, and shock signs to infer internal injury.
cues: Solid organs can bleed heavily; hollow organs can spill contents and cause peritonitis.
Pelvic injury can conceal major hemorrhage.
Blood at the urethral opening or perineal findings may indicate GU injury.
priorities: Treat shock and minimize scene time when internal bleeding is suspected.
Avoid repeated pelvic manipulation.
pitfalls: Being reassured by a soft abdomen early after injury.
Repeatedly “checking” pelvic stability.
prompts: Where can major hemorrhage occur without external blood?
What finding makes GU injury more likely?

chapters.title: Orthopaedic Trauma
chapters.hook: Musculoskeletal trauma threatens more than bones: vessels, nerves, skin, and systemic physiology may be at risk.
chapters.concept: Assess alignment, open injury, distal neurovascular status, compartment risk, associated hemorrhage, and the need for stabilization.
cues: Long-bone fractures can contribute to significant blood loss.
Dislocations can compromise nerves and vessels.
Open fractures require wound protection and careful splinting.
priorities: Check distal pulse, motor, and sensation before and after splinting.
Stabilize painful unstable injuries unless immediate transport priorities prevent delay.
pitfalls: Splinting before checking distal neurovascular status.
Forcing a limb into anatomic position despite resistance or protocol limitations.
prompts: Is there a neurovascular threat?
How did splinting change distal findings?

chapters.title: Environmental Emergencies
chapters.hook: Environmental illness is a physiology problem created or worsened by exposure.
chapters.concept: Identify heat, cold, water, altitude, pressure, electrical, venom, and wilderness hazards while preventing rescuer exposure.
cues: Heat stroke is defined by severe heat illness with CNS dysfunction.
Hypothermia can alter vital signs and resuscitation response.
Diving and altitude problems depend on pressure and oxygen physiology.
priorities: Move the patient away from the hazardous environment safely.
Treat severe temperature illness aggressively while protecting airway, ventilation, and perfusion.
pitfalls: Using fever alone to distinguish heat stroke from heat exhaustion.
Entering water, electrical, or wilderness hazards without adequate rescue resources.
prompts: What exposure mechanism explains the physiology?
What hazard threatens rescuers as well as the patient?

chapters.title: Responding to the Field Code
chapters.hook: Successful resuscitation depends on coordinated fundamentals executed with minimal interruption.
chapters.concept: Integrate high-quality CPR, rhythm recognition, defibrillation, reversible causes, airway/ventilation strategy, leadership, and post-ROSC care.
cues: Shockable and nonshockable rhythms require different immediate paths.
CPR quality and defibrillation timing strongly affect outcomes.
Reversible causes should be actively considered during the arrest, not afterward.
priorities: Assign roles and protect compression quality.
Use the rhythm and patient context to search for reversible causes.
pitfalls: Pausing compressions for prolonged procedures or discussion.
Treating the algorithm as a substitute for finding the cause.
prompts: What is stealing time from compressions?
Which reversible cause best fits this arrest?

chapters.title: Management and Resuscitation of the Critical Patient
chapters.hook: The peri-arrest patient rewards early recognition of failing compensation.
chapters.concept: Rapidly integrate airway, ventilation, perfusion, shock type, trajectory, and the most dangerous likely causes before cardiac arrest occurs.
cues: Shock can be hypovolemic, distributive, cardiogenic, or obstructive.
Compensated patients can deteriorate abruptly.
The best treatment depends on the mechanism of poor perfusion.
priorities: Identify the shock mechanism while supporting oxygen delivery.
Reassess after each intervention for improvement or unintended harm.
pitfalls: Giving the same fluid strategy to every shock state.
Waiting for profound hypotension before calling the patient critical.
prompts: What type of shock best explains the whole picture?
Which intervention helps this mechanism—and which could worsen it?

chapters.title: Obstetrics
chapters.hook: Obstetric care involves two patients connected by rapidly changing maternal physiology.
chapters.concept: Recognize normal labor, imminent delivery, hemorrhage, hypertensive emergencies, ectopic pregnancy, abnormal presentation, and trauma considerations.
cues: Maternal positioning and perfusion affect fetal perfusion.
Third-trimester bleeding can be life-threatening and should not trigger field vaginal examination.
Severe hypertension with neurologic symptoms can progress to eclampsia.
priorities: Assess maternal ABCs and pregnancy stage early.
Prepare for delivery only when birth is imminent; otherwise prioritize safe transport.
pitfalls: Performing unnecessary vaginal examination in bleeding.
Focusing on the fetus while maternal resuscitation is inadequate.
prompts: Is delivery imminent?
What maternal condition is the greatest immediate threat to both patients?

chapters.title: Neonatal Care
chapters.hook: Most newborns transition with warmth, positioning, and stimulation; a small group needs prompt ventilation-centered resuscitation.
chapters.concept: Assess term status, tone, breathing, and heart rate while preventing heat loss and escalating support according to neonatal response.
cues: Effective ventilation is the key intervention for most depressed newborns.
Heart rate is the most important response marker during resuscitation.
Prematurity and maternal/perinatal factors change risk.
priorities: Warm, position, clear obstruction only when needed, dry/stimulate, and assess.
If ventilation is ineffective, correct the ventilation before moving on.
pitfalls: Spending too long suctioning a newborn who needs ventilation.
Applying adult resuscitation logic without neonatal priorities.
prompts: Is ventilation effective?
How is the heart rate responding?

chapters.title: Pediatric Emergencies
chapters.hook: Children often fail through respiratory or shock pathways before primary cardiac arrest.
chapters.concept: Use appearance, work of breathing, circulation, age-adjusted vitals, caregiver history, and rapid reassessment to recognize deterioration early.
cues: The Pediatric Assessment Triangle offers a rapid general impression.
Bradycardia in a sick child can be a late hypoxic sign.
Children can maintain blood pressure until decompensation is advanced.
priorities: Correct oxygenation and ventilation problems early.
Use weight-based equipment and medication systems consistently.
pitfalls: Waiting for hypotension to recognize pediatric shock.
Relying on a calm child as proof that the illness is mild.
prompts: Which side of the pediatric assessment triangle is abnormal?
Is the child compensating or beginning to fail?

chapters.title: Geriatric Emergencies
chapters.hook: Older adults often present with less physiologic reserve, more medications, more comorbidity, and less textbook-like symptoms.
chapters.concept: Look for atypical ACS, infection, dehydration, medication effects, delirium, falls, frailty, and hidden injury while preserving autonomy.
cues: Normal vital signs can mask serious illness in an older adult.
Polypharmacy changes both presentation and treatment risk.
Acute confusion is not normal aging and often signals illness.
priorities: Compare with baseline function when possible.
Review medications and recent changes as part of the differential.
pitfalls: Attributing confusion or weakness to age.
Underestimating low-energy falls in frail or anticoagulated patients.
prompts: What is different from this patient’s baseline?
Which medication or comorbidity changes the risk?

chapters.title: Patients with Special Challenges
chapters.hook: Special challenges demand flexible care without lowering clinical standards.
chapters.concept: Adapt to technology dependence, tracheostomies, ventilators, LVADs, bariatric needs, developmental or sensory differences, hospice goals, abuse, poverty, and homelessness.
cues: Caregivers often know the patient’s baseline equipment and failure modes.
A patient with a continuous-flow device may not have a palpable pulse despite perfusion.
Goals of care may prioritize comfort over aggressive intervention.
priorities: Ask what is normal for this patient and device.
Respect communication needs and preexisting care plans while treating emergencies.
pitfalls: Assuming unfamiliar technology means immediate removal or disconnection.
Talking only to the caregiver when the patient can participate.
prompts: What is this patient’s baseline?
Is the problem the patient, the device, or both?

chapters.title: Transport Operations
chapters.hook: Transport safety begins before the ambulance moves and continues through decontamination and handoff.
chapters.concept: Integrate vehicle readiness, emergency driving, restraint, loading, scene positioning, air-medical decisions, infection control, and crew safety.
cues: Emergency lights and sirens do not eliminate collision risk.
Everyone should be restrained whenever operationally possible.
Air-medical use should be based on time, access, capability, and patient need.
priorities: Position the vehicle to protect the scene and create a safe work area.
Perform routine equipment and vehicle checks before calls.
pitfalls: Driving faster without considering risk versus time saved.
Standing unrestrained in the patient compartment unnecessarily.
prompts: What transport choice actually improves time to definitive care?
Where should the ambulance be positioned to protect the crew?

chapters.title: Incident Management and Mass-Casualty Incidents
chapters.hook: Large incidents require organization before individual-level optimization.
chapters.concept: Use incident command, scalable roles, triage, treatment, transport coordination, communication, and resource tracking to do the greatest good safely.
cues: The first arriving unit may need to establish command.
Triage assigns priority; it does not replace treatment.
Command structure should scale as incident complexity grows.
priorities: Declare the incident and request resources early.
Separate command, triage, treatment, and transport functions as staffing grows.
pitfalls: Becoming absorbed in the first critical patient and losing scene coordination.
Letting multiple agencies work without a common command structure.
prompts: What role is missing from the incident structure?
How does the priority change when resources are limited?

chapters.title: Vehicle Extrication and Special Rescue
chapters.hook: Rescue care is a partnership between medical priorities and technical hazard control.
chapters.concept: Coordinate stabilization, access, disentanglement, patient protection, special vehicle hazards, and rescue resources before movement.
cues: Vehicle stabilization precedes forceful disentanglement.
Modern vehicles may contain high-voltage systems, airbags, and reinforced structures.
Medical care begins as soon as safe patient access is achieved.
priorities: Work through the rescue group or incident command structure.
Protect the patient from tools, glass, movement, and environmental exposure.
pitfalls: Entering an unstable vehicle before stabilization.
Moving or cutting without communicating with the medical and rescue teams.
prompts: Is the vehicle stable?
Which rescue action could worsen the patient’s injury?

chapters.title: Hazardous Materials
chapters.hook: The safest hazmat treatment may begin with distance, identification, zones, and decontamination rather than immediate patient contact.
chapters.concept: Recognize clues, approach uphill/upwind when appropriate, establish zones, select PPE through trained resources, prevent secondary contamination, and support exposed patients after decon.
cues: Unknown substances can endanger responders and receiving hospitals.
Hot, warm, and cold zones control contamination and access.
Emergency decontamination may be required for immediate life threats.
priorities: Stage safely and use specialized resources early.
Do not move a contaminated patient into a clean ambulance.
pitfalls: Rushing into the hot zone with standard medical PPE.
Transporting contamination downstream to the crew or hospital.
prompts: Where is the safe approach and staging area?
Has the patient been adequately decontaminated for your level of PPE?

chapters.title: Terrorism Response
chapters.hook: Terrorism response adds intentionality, secondary threats, and CBRNE hazards to ordinary incident management.
chapters.concept: Recognize suspicious patterns, preserve scene safety, anticipate secondary devices, use command, and treat chemical, biologic, radiologic, nuclear, and explosive exposures within trained roles.
cues: A secondary device may target responders after the initial event.
Biologic attacks may first appear as unusual illness patterns rather than a dramatic scene.
Syndromic surveillance can help detect emerging events.
priorities: Maintain situational awareness even after patient contact.
Use specialized hazmat and law-enforcement resources rather than exceeding training.
pitfalls: Clustering all responders near the obvious scene.
Assuming every terrorist event will be immediately recognizable.
prompts: What makes this scene suspicious rather than accidental?
Where could a secondary threat be placed?

chapters.title: Disaster Response
chapters.hook: Disaster readiness is built before the event and continues through recovery.
chapters.concept: Use an all-hazards approach to preparedness, command, resource management, responder sustainment, public communication, recovery, and after-action improvement.
cues: Disasters can overwhelm normal local resources.
Mutual aid and interoperable command should be planned before need.
After-action review converts experience into preparedness.
priorities: Plan for staffing, communications, supplies, transport, and responder needs.
Track resource status and maintain operational periods during prolonged events.
pitfalls: Building plans around one specific disaster only.
Ignoring responder fatigue and logistics during long operations.
prompts: Which capability fails first if the incident lasts 72 hours?
What should change after the after-action review?

chapters.title: Crime Scene Awareness
chapters.hook: Patient care and personal safety occur inside a scene that may contain violence, evidence, and law-enforcement priorities.
chapters.concept: Use scene size-up, safe approach, cover/concealment awareness, retreat options, evidence preservation, documentation, and trafficking/abuse awareness without compromising urgent care.
cues: Tunnel vision on the patient can hide escalating scene danger.
Evidence should be disturbed only as necessary for lifesaving care.
Law enforcement controls security; EMS controls medical care within safe access.
priorities: Keep a path of retreat and maintain communication.
Document unavoidable movement or alteration of evidence when relevant.
pitfalls: Entering an unsecured violent scene because a patient is visible.
Handling weapons or evidence that does not need to be moved.
prompts: What is your exit if the scene becomes unsafe?
What can you preserve without delaying lifesaving care?

cases.title: Silent Chest

steps: Severe work of breathing, poor speech, falling air movement, hypoxemia, fatigue.

Aggressive protocol-based bronchodilation, oxygenation, assisted ventilation when needed, rapid transport, prepare advanced airway rescue.

Treat the failing oxygenation and cardiac physiology rather than the wheeze alone.

cases.title: Bus Crash, Ten Patients
cases.scene: Your unit arrives first to a school bus collision. At least ten patients are visible, traffic is active, and bystanders are moving among the injured.
steps: Multiple patients, active hazards, resource mismatch, unstructured bystander activity.
The incident requires command and resource organization before one-patient care absorbs the first crew.
Mass-casualty incident requiring scalable incident command.
Establish/announce command, request resources, define safe access, initiate triage, assign arriving units to functional roles.
Create structure early so treatment and transport can scale.
Patient count, hazards, resource status, triage distribution, transport destinations.

cases.title: Unknown Vapor
cases.scene: Several workers stumble out of a warehouse coughing and tearing. A visible vapor cloud is near an open loading door. One patient collapses just inside.
cases.vitals: Unknown substance • wind moving toward the parking lot
steps: Multiple similar patients, visible vapor, active release, contaminated area.
Unprotected entry could create additional victims and contaminate the ambulance/hospital.
Stage upwind/uphill as appropriate, establish command, request hazmat, isolate zones, prepare for decontaminated patients.
Do not enter the hot zone without appropriate training and PPE.
Wind/source changes, zone integrity, patient flow, contamination status, responder symptoms.

cases.title: The High-Risk Refusal
cases.scene: A 58-year-old with pressure-like chest discomfort now feels better after resting and refuses transport because of work obligations.
steps: Potentially time-sensitive cardiac symptoms despite temporary improvement.
Symptom resolution does not rule out acute coronary syndrome; refusal requires capacity and informed risk discussion.
High-risk refusal in a patient with possible ACS.
Assess capacity, explain specific risks and alternatives, involve medical control/support persons as appropriate, offer continued care and transport.
Do not reduce the refusal process to a signature; document findings, discussion, and patient decision.
Confirm understanding, repeat key risks, provide return precautions and reassess before leaving.

cases.title: Silent Chest, Fading Patient
cases.scene: A 24-year-old with severe asthma is exhausted, speaks one word at a time, and now has minimal air movement with increasing drowsiness.
steps: Decreasing wheeze with poor air movement, fatigue, altered mentation, hypoxemia.
The patient is progressing from respiratory distress to ventilatory failure.
Impending respiratory arrest from severe bronchospasm.
Aggressive oxygenation/ventilatory support, protocol-directed bronchodilator therapy, prepare advanced airway strategy, rapid transport.
Support ventilation before complete arrest develops.
Mental status, tidal volume, air movement, SpO2, ETCO2 when available, response to therapy.

cases.title: Cannot Intubate, Oxygen Falling
cases.scene: After two unsuccessful intubation attempts in a critically ill patient, oxygen saturation is falling and bag-mask ventilation is becoming difficult.
steps: Repeated airway attempts, worsening oxygenation, increasingly difficult ventilation.
The priority is oxygenation, not completing a preferred airway technique.
Failed airway pathway with imminent hypoxic injury.

Return to best oxygenation technique, optimize positioning and adjuncts, use supraglottic rescue if indicated, limit repeated attempts, prepare surgical airway only when truly cannot oxygenate/ventilate per protocol.
Stop fixation on intubation and restore oxygenation.
SpO2 trend, chest rise, capnography, mask seal, airway patency, hemodynamics.

cases.title: Sudden Collapse After Chest Trauma
cases.scene: A 31-year-old struck in the chest becomes rapidly dyspneic and hypotensive. Breath sounds are markedly reduced on the left with distended neck veins.
steps: Trauma, unilateral breath-sound reduction, severe respiratory distress, shock.
The pattern suggests pressure obstructing venous return and ventilation.
Immediate protocol-directed decompression, oxygenation/ventilation support, rapid transport.
Treat the life threat based on the clinical pattern rather than waiting for imaging.
Perfusion, breath sounds, work of breathing, SpO2, blood pressure, recurrence.

cases.title: Fever, Confusion, Low Pressure
cases.scene: A 72-year-old from home has fever, confusion, warm skin, and weakness after several days of urinary symptoms.
steps: Suspected infection plus altered mentation, tachypnea, and hypotension.
The patient shows infection-associated organ dysfunction and poor perfusion.
Support oxygenation, obtain vascular access, protocol-directed fluid resuscitation with reassessment, consider vasopressor pathway if indicated, early sepsis notification and transport.
Treat perfusion failure while avoiding delays in transport.
Pressure/MAP trend, mental status, lung sounds, capillary refill, urine history, response to fluids.

cases.title: Deep Breathing and Abdominal Pain
cases.scene: A 19-year-old with diabetes has vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, and deep rapid respirations.
cases.vitals: HR 124 • RR 30 deep • BP 96/58 • glucose HIGH
steps: Hyperglycemia, dehydration, Kussmaul-type respirations, GI symptoms.
The breathing pattern is compensatory for metabolic acidosis, not primary respiratory disease.
Support airway/oxygenation as needed, vascular access, protocol-directed isotonic fluid, monitor ECG and mental status, transport.
Do not suppress compensatory ventilation unless ventilation actually fails.
Perfusion, mentation, glucose trend, ECG, respiratory effort, signs of cerebral deterioration.

cases.title: Seizure That Will Not Stop
cases.scene: A 44-year-old has continuous generalized seizure activity for more than 5 minutes without regaining consciousness.
steps: Prolonged seizure, hypoxemia, no recovery of consciousness.
Ongoing seizure activity threatens oxygenation and causes metabolic injury.
Protect airway, oxygenate/ventilate, protocol-directed benzodiazepine therapy, check glucose, identify reversible causes, transport.
Treat sustained seizure promptly while supporting ventilation.
Cessation of motor activity, ventilation, SpO2/ETCO2, glucose, postictal neurologic status.

cases.title: Last Known Well
cases.scene: A 67-year-old develops sudden aphasia and right arm weakness while eating breakfast. Family knows the exact onset time.
steps: Abrupt focal neurologic deficit with known onset and normal glucose.
Time-dependent reperfusion decisions require rapid recognition and destination planning.
Perform validated stroke assessment, establish last-known-well, check glucose, minimize scene delay, select appropriate stroke destination, pre-notify.
Protect time; do not delay transport for nonessential interventions.
Neurologic changes, airway, glucose, hemodynamics, transport timeline.

cases.title: Hives, Wheeze, and Shock
cases.scene: Minutes after a bee sting, a 35-year-old develops diffuse hives, wheezing, hoarse voice, and dizziness.
steps: Rapid allergic symptoms involving airway/respiratory system and hypotension.
Multisystem involvement after allergen exposure indicates anaphylaxis.
Immediate protocol-directed IM epinephrine, airway/oxygenation support, vascular access and fluids, adjuncts without delaying epinephrine, rapid transport.
Give epinephrine early when anaphylaxis is recognized.
Voice/airway, work of breathing, wheeze, blood pressure, skin findings, need for repeat epinephrine per protocol.

cases.title: Pinpoint Pupils, Slow Breathing
cases.scene: A 29-year-old is unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and respirations of 4/min after suspected opioid use.
steps: Severe hypoventilation, altered consciousness, opioid toxidrome clues.
The immediate threat is inadequate ventilation and hypoxemia.
Open airway, ventilate with oxygen, protocol-directed naloxone titrated to adequate breathing, monitor for recurrence and coingestants.
Ventilate first; naloxone is an adjunct to restoring breathing.
Respiratory rate/depth, SpO2, ETCO2, mental status, recurrence after naloxone.

cases.title: Bleeding After Delivery
cases.scene: Ten minutes after an uncomplicated field delivery, the mother develops heavy vaginal bleeding and feels faint. The uterus feels soft.
steps: Heavy postpartum bleeding, boggy uterus, shock.
Uterine atony is a common cause of postpartum hemorrhage.
Uterine massage, protocol-directed uterotonic therapy when authorized, vascular access/fluids, rapid transport, keep newborn and mother appropriately managed.
Bleeding rate, uterine tone, pressure, mental status, perfusion, response to interventions.

cases.title: Child With Retractions
cases.scene: A 3-year-old has fever, cough, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, and decreasing interaction with parents.
steps: Increased work of breathing, hypoxemia, reduced interaction.
Children can compensate until fatigue leads to rapid deterioration.
Pediatric respiratory distress progressing toward failure.
Position of comfort, oxygen, suction if needed, age-appropriate ventilation support, minimize agitation, rapid transport.
Use appearance, work of breathing, and circulation to skin to trend severity.
Mental status, effort, respiratory rate, chest rise, SpO2, heart rate.

cases.title: Quiet Infant With Fever
cases.scene: A 2-month-old with fever is unusually sleepy, feeds poorly, and has mottled skin with weak peripheral pulses.
cases.vitals: HR 190 • RR 52 • cap refill 5 sec • Temp 38.7°C
steps: Young infant, fever, poor feeding, lethargy, poor perfusion.
Infants may show nonspecific signs despite serious infection.
Support airway/oxygenation, keep warm, vascular access if feasible without delaying transport, protocol-directed fluid, rapid pediatric-capable destination.
Treat abnormal appearance and perfusion as high risk.
Mental status, capillary refill, pulses, heart rate, work of breathing, glucose when indicated.

cases.title: Burned in a Closed Room
cases.scene: A patient rescued from a house fire has facial burns, soot around the mouth, hoarseness, and progressive coughing.
steps: Enclosed-space fire, facial burns, soot, voice change.
Pulse oximetry may not reveal carbon monoxide exposure; airway edema can progress.
Inhalation injury with risk of airway compromise and toxic gas exposure.
High-concentration oxygen, early airway planning, cardiac/CO monitoring if available, assess for cyanide risk in severe enclosed-space fire, burn care and transport.
Anticipate deterioration before edema makes airway management harder.
Voice, stridor, work of breathing, mental status, airway swelling, hemodynamics.

cases.title: Pinned for Two Hours
cases.scene: A construction worker has a leg trapped under concrete for two hours. Rescue crews are preparing to lift the slab.
steps: Reperfusion can release potassium, acids, and myoglobin, causing dysrhythmia and shock.
Coordinate with rescue, establish monitoring and vascular access, protocol-directed fluids before release when feasible, prepare for hyperkalemia management, rapid transport.
Plan treatment before the load is removed.
ECG changes, blood pressure, mental status, limb findings, time of release.

cases.title: Agitated and Hallucinating
cases.scene: A 33-year-old is intensely agitated, paranoid, diaphoretic, and physically combative after an unknown substance exposure.
steps: Severe agitation plus autonomic activation and hyperthermia.
Medical/toxic causes may underlie dangerous behavior and can rapidly become fatal.
Excited/agitated delirium syndrome from stimulant/toxic/metabolic cause requiring emergency medical management.
Scene safety, de-escalation when possible, rapid team-based control per protocol, monitor airway/ventilation, temperature, glucose and cardiac rhythm, treat hyperthermia and complications.
Avoid prolonged physical struggle; treat physiologic threats.
Temperature, ETCO2/ventilation, oxygenation, rhythm, mental status, restraint complications.

cases.title: Explosion With Hidden Injuries
cases.scene: After an industrial explosion, a walking patient complains only of ear pain and mild shortness of breath. Clothing is intact and there is no major external bleeding.
steps: Blast exposure, tympanic symptoms, respiratory complaint despite limited external injury.
Primary blast injury can damage lungs and other gas-containing organs without obvious wounds.
Oxygen as indicated, careful respiratory assessment, avoid false reassurance from minimal external trauma, monitor for deterioration, appropriate trauma destination.
Treat mechanism as a clue to hidden injury.
Work of breathing, SpO2, lung sounds, chest pain, neurologic status, evolving signs.

cases.title: Weakness With Wide QRS
cases.scene: A dialysis patient who missed treatment reports weakness and palpitations. The ECG shows tall peaked T waves with QRS widening.
steps: Renal failure, missed dialysis, weakness, bradycardia, hyperkalemic ECG changes.
Membrane instability can progress to lethal dysrhythmia.
Protocol-directed membrane stabilization and potassium-shifting therapy, cardiac monitoring, vascular access, urgent transport.
Treat ECG toxicity promptly according to protocol.
QRS width, T-wave morphology, heart rate, perfusion, rhythm changes.

ecgs.name: Normal Sinus Rhythm
ecgs.criteria: Regular rhythm, upright P before every QRS, consistent PR, narrow QRS.
ecgs.pearl: Start every interpretation with rate, regularity, P waves, PR, and QRS width.

ecgs.name: Sinus Bradycardia
ecgs.criteria: Sinus pattern at a slow rate.
ecgs.pearl: Treat only when the bradycardia is causing clinically important poor perfusion.

ecgs.name: Sinus Tachycardia
ecgs.criteria: Sinus pattern at a fast rate.
ecgs.pearl: Search for the driver: pain, fever, hypovolemia, hypoxia, anxiety, sepsis, etc.

ecgs.name: Sinus Arrhythmia
ecgs.criteria: Sinus beats with cyclic variation in R–R interval.
ecgs.pearl: Often respiratory and benign; confirm normal P-QRS relationship.

ecgs.name: Atrial Fibrillation
ecgs.criteria: Irregularly irregular rhythm without consistent P waves.
ecgs.pearl: Rate and perfusion matter; new AF may reflect acute illness.

ecgs.name: Atrial Flutter
ecgs.criteria: Organized atrial activity with sawtooth flutter waves; ventricular conduction may be fixed or variable.
ecgs.pearl: A ventricular rate near 150 should raise suspicion for 2:1 flutter.

ecgs.name: SVT / Regular Narrow Tachycardia
ecgs.criteria: Very regular narrow-complex tachycardia; P waves may be hidden.
ecgs.pearl: Assess stability first, then use rhythm-specific protocol.

ecgs.name: Junctional Rhythm
ecgs.criteria: Narrow rhythm with absent, inverted, or retrograde P waves.
ecgs.pearl: Consider why the sinus node or atrial impulse is not controlling the rate.

ecgs.name: Accelerated Junctional Rhythm
ecgs.criteria: Junctional morphology at a faster escape/automatic rate.
ecgs.pearl: Context and patient perfusion determine significance.

ecgs.name: First-Degree AV Block
ecgs.criteria: Every P conducts, but PR interval is prolonged and constant.
ecgs.pearl: It is a conduction delay, not dropped beats.

ecgs.name: Mobitz I (Wenckebach)
ecgs.criteria: PR progressively lengthens until a QRS is dropped.
ecgs.pearl: Look for grouped beating and repeating PR progression.

ecgs.name: Mobitz II
ecgs.criteria: Constant PR intervals with intermittent nonconducted P waves.
ecgs.pearl: More likely to deteriorate to complete block; symptoms increase urgency.

ecgs.name: Third-Degree AV Block
ecgs.criteria: P waves and QRS complexes occur independently.
ecgs.pearl: Recognize AV dissociation and assess for low-output instability.

ecgs.name: Premature Ventricular Complexes
ecgs.criteria: Early wide bizarre ventricular beat without a preceding normal P wave.
ecgs.pearl: PVCs are findings; treat the patient and underlying cause, not isolated ectopy.

ecgs.name: Ventricular Bigeminy
ecgs.criteria: A repeating pattern of normal beat followed by PVC.
ecgs.pearl: Check perfusion and possible triggers such as ischemia or electrolyte disturbance.

ecgs.name: Monomorphic Ventricular Tachycardia
ecgs.criteria: Regular wide-complex tachycardia with similar QRS morphology.
ecgs.pearl: If uncertain, a regular wide tachycardia should be treated as VT until proven otherwise.

ecgs.name: Torsades de Pointes
ecgs.criteria: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QRS amplitude appearing to twist around the baseline.
ecgs.pearl: Think prolonged QT and protocol-specific magnesium/defibrillation decisions depending on pulse and stability.

ecgs.name: Ventricular Fibrillation
ecgs.criteria: Chaotic ventricular electrical activity with no organized QRS complexes.
ecgs.pearl: Shockable cardiac-arrest rhythm: high-quality CPR and rapid defibrillation are central.

ecgs.name: Fine Ventricular Fibrillation
ecgs.criteria: Low-amplitude chaotic activity that can resemble asystole.
ecgs.pearl: Verify lead contact and gain; do not mistake artifact or fine VF for a flat line.

ecgs.name: Asystole
ecgs.criteria: Near-flat tracing without organized ventricular activity.
ecgs.pearl: Confirm in more than one lead and check equipment before labeling asystole.

ecgs.name: Pulseless Electrical Activity
ecgs.criteria: Organized electrical rhythm with no palpable pulse.
ecgs.pearl: PEA is a clinical diagnosis: treat arrest and search aggressively for reversible causes.

ecgs.name: Ventricular Paced Rhythm
ecgs.criteria: Pacing spikes followed by wide paced QRS complexes when capture is present.
ecgs.pearl: Electrical capture must be paired with mechanical capture and improved perfusion.

ecgs.name: Hyperkalemia Pattern
ecgs.criteria: Progressive potassium toxicity may produce peaked T waves, PR/QRS changes, and eventual sine-wave morphology.
ecgs.pearl: Always interpret ECG changes with renal history and the patient’s overall condition.

ecgs.name: Inferior STEMI Pattern
ecgs.criteria: ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal changes possible in I/aVL.
ecgs.pearl: Consider right-sided involvement when hypotension or RV clues are present.

ecgs.name: Anterior STEMI Pattern
ecgs.criteria: ST elevation across anterior precordial leads, often V1–V4 depending on territory.
ecgs.pearl: Large anterior injury patterns can carry significant pump-failure risk.

ecgs.name: Lateral STEMI Pattern
ecgs.criteria: ST elevation in I, aVL, V5–V6 depending on territory.
ecgs.pearl: Look for reciprocal changes and contiguous-lead patterns.

ecgs.name: Posterior MI Clues
ecgs.criteria: ST depression and tall R waves in anterior leads can be reciprocal signs of posterior injury.
ecgs.pearl: Posterior leads can clarify the pattern when clinically indicated.

ecgs.name: Right Ventricular MI Clues
ecgs.criteria: Inferior injury plus right-sided ST elevation can indicate RV involvement.
ecgs.pearl: Perfusion can be preload sensitive; integrate lungs, JVD, pressure, and right-sided leads.

ecgs.name: Atrial Tachycardia
ecgs.criteria: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia with abnormal atrial P-wave morphology before QRS complexes.
ecgs.pearl: Differentiate from sinus tachycardia by P-wave morphology and clinical context.

ecgs.name: Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia
ecgs.criteria: Irregular narrow rhythm with at least three distinct P-wave morphologies and rate over 100.
ecgs.pearl: Often occurs in significant pulmonary disease; treat the underlying cause.

ecgs.name: Wandering Atrial Pacemaker
ecgs.criteria: Irregular rhythm with at least three P-wave morphologies at a rate under 100.
ecgs.pearl: Rate distinguishes it from multifocal atrial tachycardia.

ecgs.name: Idioventricular Rhythm
ecgs.criteria: Slow wide-complex ventricular escape rhythm, often 20–40/min.
ecgs.pearl: Assess perfusion and search for causes of failed supraventricular impulse formation or conduction.

ecgs.name: Accelerated Idioventricular Rhythm
ecgs.criteria: Wide ventricular rhythm around 40–100/min, usually regular.
ecgs.pearl: Can appear during reperfusion; context and hemodynamics matter.

ecgs.name: Right Bundle Branch Block
ecgs.criteria: Wide QRS with terminal rightward forces, classically an rSR' pattern in V1 and broad terminal S waves laterally.
ecgs.pearl: A new conduction abnormality should be interpreted with symptoms and ischemic context.

ecgs.name: Left Bundle Branch Block
ecgs.criteria: Wide QRS with broad/notched lateral R waves and deep anterior S waves with secondary ST-T changes.
ecgs.pearl: LBBB complicates ischemia interpretation; use contemporary criteria and clinical context.

ecgs.name: Pre-excitation / WPW Pattern
ecgs.criteria: Short PR interval, delta wave, and widened initial QRS upstroke.
ecgs.pearl: Irregular wide tachycardia with pre-excitation is a high-risk pattern; avoid AV-nodal-only treatment pathways.

ecgs.name: Prolonged QT Pattern
ecgs.criteria: QT interval is prolonged relative to rate, increasing torsades risk.
ecgs.pearl: Look for medications, electrolytes, congenital causes, and bradycardia.

ecgs.name: Pericarditis Pattern
ecgs.criteria: Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression rather than a single coronary territory pattern.
ecgs.pearl: Clinical context and reciprocal changes help distinguish pericarditis from STEMI.

ecgs.name: Benign Early Repolarization Pattern
ecgs.criteria: J-point/ST elevation, often precordial, with stable morphology in an otherwise appropriate clinical context.
ecgs.pearl: Do not label ST elevation benign without integrating symptoms, prior ECGs, and reciprocal changes.

ecgs.name: LVH With Strain
ecgs.criteria: High QRS voltage with secondary ST-T repolarization abnormalities.
ecgs.pearl: Voltage plus discordant repolarization can mimic ischemia; compare with symptoms and prior tracings.

ecgs.name: Digoxin Effect
ecgs.criteria: Scooped downsloping ST depression with shortened QT may appear during therapeutic digoxin effect.
ecgs.pearl: The ECG effect alone does not equal digoxin toxicity.

ecgs.name: Subendocardial Ischemia Pattern
ecgs.criteria: Horizontal or downsloping ST depression in contiguous leads may reflect ischemia.
ecgs.pearl: Dynamic changes plus symptoms are more concerning than a single static tracing.

ecgs.name: Hyperacute T-Wave Pattern
ecgs.criteria: Broad, bulky, disproportionate T waves may precede obvious ST elevation in acute coronary occlusion.
ecgs.pearl: Serial ECGs matter when symptoms are concerning and the first tracing is nondiagnostic.

ecgs.name: Hypokalemia Pattern
ecgs.criteria: Flattened T waves, ST depression, and prominent U waves may appear with low potassium.
ecgs.pearl: Electrolyte abnormalities can create both electrical and muscular symptoms.

ecgs.name: Pacemaker Failure to Capture
ecgs.criteria: Pacing spikes are present but are not consistently followed by depolarization/QRS complexes.
ecgs.pearl: Confirm both electrical and mechanical capture after any pacing intervention.

ecgs.name: Pacemaker Failure to Sense
ecgs.criteria: Pacing spikes occur inappropriately despite intrinsic cardiac activity.
ecgs.pearl: Poor sensing can create dangerous competition with native rhythm; assess patient and device function.

ecgs.name: Motion / Electrode Artifact
ecgs.criteria: Baseline disturbance can mimic dysrhythmia while organized complexes continue through the artifact.
ecgs.pearl: Always correlate the monitor with the patient and a pulse before treating the screen.

ecgs.name: Brugada-like Pattern
ecgs.criteria: Coved ST elevation in right precordial leads with a characteristic conduction/repolarization pattern.
ecgs.pearl: Syncope or arrest with this pattern warrants urgent specialty evaluation; do not confuse it with routine RBBB.
